head:
Adults · Activity

The adult body in the age of the chair

You may exercise two or three times a week and spend the rest of your waking life sitting. Does Tuesday's session make up for the chair from Monday to Friday? This article asks the question, answers it in six steps that run from the most general to the most precise, then says what you can put in place.

The question

For many adults, most of the day is now spent on a chair: at work, in the car or on the train, in front of a screen, then on the sofa. Exercise has become a separate activity, slotted into a time window of the week.

This arrangement raises a problem that exercise alone may not solve. First, two notions that are often confused need to be told apart. The World Health Organization (WHO) defines physical activity as any bodily movement produced by the muscles that requires energy. It defines sedentary behaviour as any waking period with low energy expenditure: sitting, reclining or lying down.1 These are not the two ends of one scale. You can run for 30 minutes in the morning, then sit in a chair for nine hours: you are both active and sedentary.

If moving is enough, the solution is simple: do your session, and the rest of the day does not matter. If sitting time has an effect of its own, then the whole day has to change, not just the training slot. The two answers lead to very different behaviour. It is therefore worth finding out which one is right, rather than repeating "move more" or "don't sit" without knowing.

The question

When you spend most of your day sitting, are your exercise sessions enough to protect your health? If not, what needs to change, and by how much?

What is at stake

According to the WHO, insufficiently active adults have a 20 to 30% higher risk of death than sufficiently active adults.1 This figure describes an association between two groups, not what will happen to you, but it gives the order of magnitude: the way you move weighs on how long you live.

That is not all. According to the same fact sheet, in adults activity is linked to a lower risk of cardiovascular death, type 2 diabetes and falls, to better sleep, to better mental and cognitive health, and to fewer symptoms of depression and anxiety.1 What is at stake is extra years, and years in which you stay able to get around, sleep and concentrate.

The stakes are growing. The WHO estimates that 31% of adults, about 1.8 billion people, did not reach the recommended level in 2022. The share has risen by about 5 points since 2010 and would reach 35% in 2030 if the trend continues.2

There is also something at stake for someone who trains: if only exercise counts, you have done the essential; if your seated day counts too, part of your effort misses what matters. This is what the article sets out to settle.

Finally, untested advice gives false security or discourages for nothing. Telling someone they are "protected" by their three weekly sessions while they sit ten hours a day would be a mistake if the data say otherwise. Telling them to change everything, when a few minutes are enough, would discourage them.
rest:
The path of the demonstration

We start from the whole population and move towards increasingly precise questions. At each step, one point to prove, one piece of evidence chosen and read, then what it changes for you.

  1. How many adults are concerned, and which ones.
  2. What sitting time does to the risk of death, measured by a sensor.
  3. Does exercise cancel out the chair?
  4. Why the chair would act: what happens in the body.
  5. How much movement is needed.
  6. What can distort all of this, and what remains uncertain.
Step 1 of 6

A whole-population problem, with a specific profile

What we want to establish: the chair and the lack of activity do not concern a minority.

The largest published analysis pools 507 surveys of the adult population and 5.7 million participants in 163 countries and territories. It calls an adult "insufficiently active" if they do not do, per week, 150 minutes of moderate activity, 75 minutes of vigorous activity or an equivalent combination.3 Moderate activity is an effort in which you breathe faster without being out of breath, such as a brisk walk.

The share of adults who move too little rose from 2000 to 2022

Adults with insufficient physical activity, age-standardised values. The axis runs from 0 to 40% and the points are placed according to the years. Source: Strain et al., Lancet Global Health, 2024 (abstract).3

What this means

In 2022, 31.3% of the world's adults were below this threshold, against 23.4% in 2000: about 8 points more in 22 years (editorial calculation). This analysis measures activity, not sitting, so it does not prove that the chair is the cause. It shows that daily movement is declining, and that if you are below the threshold, you are one of one adult in three.

Another large analysis (2018: 358 surveys, 168 countries, 1.9 million participants) finds 28.5% in 2001 and 27.5% in 2016, a decline judged not significant.4 The surveys, the period and the model differ, and the open abstracts do not explain the difference in level. Both place the share below the threshold between 23 and 29% in the early 2000s, and neither sees an improvement: one observes a rise, the other stability.

In France, in INCA 3 from Anses (3,157 adults aged 18 to 79, 2014-2015), more than 80% of adults spend at least 3 hours a day in sedentary activities, and their leisure screen time rose by about 1 hour 20 minutes a day in seven years.6 In Esteban (2,682 adults, 2014-2016), nearly 80% of men and women spend more than 3 hours a day in front of a screen outside work.7 These are questionnaires, not sensors. The activity level also depends on the threshold: 71% of men and 53% of women meet the French guidelines in Esteban,7 but Anses, which combines several criteria (cardiorespiratory activity, strengthening, flexibility, less than 8 hours sitting a day), counts only 5% of adults as sufficiently active.5 A percentage of "active" adults means nothing without its threshold.

Who is most affected?

The groups are not alike. In 2022, 33.8% of women and 28.7% of men had insufficient activity.3 The link with wealth is counter-intuitive: in 2016, the share reached 36.8% in high-income countries against 16.2% in low-income countries.4 The open sources do not give the cause. One hypothesis, not demonstrated here: where many adults walk or have a physical job, fewer of them fall below the threshold without doing sport.

In France, in INCA 3, 89% of 18-44 year-olds spend at least 3 hours a day in sedentary activities, against 72% of 65-79 year-olds, and 52% of those with a degree at bac+4 or above are sedentary for more than 7 hours a day, against 30% of adults with primary or lower-secondary education.6

What this means

The profile most exposed to the chair resembles that of an adult aged 18 to 44, with a degree, who walks little to get around, and probably that of an office job. If that is you, the question of this article concerns you first. This reading is the editorial team's: the surveys describe groups, not occupations.

The population is therefore affected on a massive scale. What remains is to find out whether this sitting time does something measurable to health, independently of everything else.

Step 2 of 6

Sitting time tracks the risk of death, even when measured by a sensor

What we want to establish: sitting time is associated with a higher risk, and not only because people get it wrong when they report it.

Almost all studies on sedentary behaviour rely on what people report, which leaves doubt about the accuracy of the figures. An analysis of 8 studies therefore used a movement sensor (accelerometer) worn during the day, in 36,383 adults with a mean age of 62.6 years, followed for a median of 5.8 years (2,149 deaths). They were classified into four equal groups, from least to most sedentary, then from least to most active.8

The more you sit, the higher the risk of death; the more you move around, the lower it is

Relative risk of death, the first quartile of each group being 1.00 (model B of the study). 2,149 deaths in total. Source: Ekelund et al., BMJ, 2019.8

What this means

The most sedentary quartile had 2.63 times the risk of death of the least sedentary quartile (confidence interval 1.94 to 3.56), and this risk rises at each step: 1.28, 1.71, then 2.63.8 The right-hand side of the chart shows the reverse: the quartile doing the most light activity has a risk of 0.38, nearly three times lower than the one that moves the least. What matters is therefore not only the chair, but all the movement it replaces. In this model, sedentary time and moderate-to-vigorous activity are adjusted for each other: the effect of the chair is therefore not explained only by a lack of exercise.

The authors note where the risk becomes clear. A significant excess mortality appears from 9.5 sedentary hours a day. On the smoothed curves, the risk is 1.48 times the reference at 10 hours and 2.92 times at 12 hours.8 In the other direction, the maximum risk reduction lies around 375 minutes a day of light activity (6 h 15) and around 24 minutes a day of moderate-to-vigorous activity.8

This study is not isolated. A review of 47 articles (Biswas, 2015), which retains only results adjusted for activity, associates sedentary time with more all-cause deaths (risk ratio of 1.24, i.e. 24% more) and above all with more type 2 diabetes (1.91). Sedentary time is self-reported in all the articles but one.9 A meta-analysis of 34 studies and 1,331,468 participants (Patterson, 2018) refines the curve: up to 8 hours sitting a day, each additional hour comes with 1% more risk of death, beyond 8 hours with 4%.10 Sensor, questionnaires and dose-response curve draw the same shape: the risk rises, and faster in long seated days.

The association therefore holds when position is measured with a sensor. But these studies adjust for activity. The real question is then more precise: when you move a lot otherwise, does the risk from the chair disappear?

Step 3 of 6

Does exercise erase the chair?

What we want to establish: how far activity offsets sitting time, and at what volume.

To answer this, a team from the University of Cambridge pooled 16 studies, i.e. 1,005,791 participants and 84,609 deaths, with harmonised data. They were mostly aged 45 or over.11,12 Its main result: in the most active people, the equivalent of 60 to 75 minutes a day of moderate activity, sitting 8 hours a day or more was not associated with an increased risk of death. In the least active, deaths were 28 to 59% more frequent than in the most active quartile.11,12

This volume needs translating. Sixty to seventy-five minutes a day make 7 to 8 h 45 a week, about 3 times the WHO guideline of 150 minutes (editorial calculation). About three participants in four did not reach this level.11 Three 45-minute sessions make 135 minutes: the public health guideline, far from the level at which the excess risk disappears.

The same report gives a borderline case, that of television. Watching more than 5 hours of television a day is associated with a 93% increased risk in the least active, and 16% in the most active.12

Even in the most active, long hours of television keep some risk

Increased risk of death associated with more than 5 hours of television a day. The report does not specify the exact comparison group: reading to be confirmed in the original article. Source: Ekelund et al., Lancet, 2016, via TCTMD (specialist press report).12

What this means

Very high activity strongly reduces the risk linked to sitting time, but not necessarily to zero in every situation, and the gap between an inactive person and a very active one is huge (93% against 16%). For you, two lessons. First, a long evening in front of a screen is not neutral, even if you have trained. Second, the activity level that erases the excess in this study is well above three sessions a week, and it assumes movement every day, not only isolated sessions.

Biswas, however, observes sedentary time associated with increased risks after adjustment for activity, more clearly when activity is low.9 The editorial team's reading: the more you move, the smaller the effect of the chair, without our being able to say, with these sources, at what volume it disappears for each person.

It remains to understand why a chair would have an effect. Something must happen in the body. The next two experiments make it possible to see it.

Step 4 of 6

Why the chair acts: what happens in the body

What we want to establish: a plausible mechanism exists, observed in trials in which movement was varied.

Observational studies cannot demonstrate a cause. Trials, on the other hand, impose the change. The first is a randomised crossover trial (Dunstan, 2012). Nineteen overweight or obese adults, aged 45 to 65, spent three times five hours in the laboratory, after drinking a standard drink rich in sugar and fat: once sitting without interruption, once with 2 minutes of slow walking every 20 minutes, once with 2 minutes of faster walking every 20 minutes.13

Two minutes of walking every 20 minutes lower the rise in blood sugar

Incremental area under the blood glucose curve over 5 hours, 19 adults who completed all three sessions. Source: Dunstan et al., Diabetes Care, 2012 (full text).13

What this means

When you stay seated after a meal, blood glucose rises higher. Breaking up the position with 2 minutes of walking every 20 minutes reduced this rise by 24.1% (slow walking) and by 29.6% (faster walking). The insulin response fell by about 23% in both cases.13 For you, this means that even a brief, slow break changes the way your body reacts to a meal. It is an effect lasting a few hours, measured in a laboratory, not proof about lifespan.

The second trial (Knudsen, 2012) imposed the lack of movement. Nine healthy young men went from 10,000 to about 1,500 steps a day for 14 days, while eating 50% more calories. Their insulin sensitivity had already dropped by the third day; by the fourteenth, the glucose infusion rate needed to maintain their blood glucose had fallen by about 44% and visceral fat (around the organs) had increased. On the thirtieth day, insulin sensitivity had returned to its baseline level, but weight and total adiposity remained higher.14 Clear limits: nine participants, overfeeding at the same time as inactivity, abstract only read. We do not know how much comes from the lack of steps and how much from the calories.

Type 2 diabetes is precisely the outcome for which Biswas finds the strongest association with sedentary time (1.91).9 The results point in the same direction: the body responds less well to insulin when you move less, and this change appears quickly.

What this means

The mechanism is plausible and can be observed within a few days. It also seems reversible: on the thirtieth day, insulin sensitivity had returned to its baseline level. This does not prove that the chair causes deaths. It is what makes the association in step 2 credible: we can see how the body could suffer the consequences.

If the effect exists and movement counters it, the question becomes practical: how much movement, exactly, to get most of the benefit?

Step 5 of 6

How much movement is needed

What we want to establish: where the biggest gain lies, and where the curve flattens.

The most telling measure is the number of steps per day. A meta-analysis of 15 cohorts (Paluch, 2022) followed 47,471 adults wearing a step counter, for a median of 7.1 years, with 3,013 deaths. They are divided into four equal groups according to their daily step count, compared with the least active group.15

The first thousands of steps are the ones that pay off the most

Adjusted hazard ratios for all-cause death, 15 cohorts, 47,471 adults, 3,013 deaths. Heights equal to the published hazard ratios (intervals: 0.51 to 0.71; 0.49 to 0.62; 0.39 to 0.57). Source: Paluch et al., Lancet Public Health, 2022 (full text).15

What this means

Moving from the least active quartile (median of 3,553 steps) to the next (5,801 steps) corresponds to a risk of death 40% lower (ratio of 0.60). The gap between these two levels is about 2,250 steps (editorial calculation), or in the order of 20 more minutes of walking a day (at about 100 steps per minute, editorial estimate). The following steps add less: 0.55, then 0.47. For you, this means that the biggest step is the first, and that you do not need to wait until you have an hour to spare before starting.15

The authors also locate where the curve flattens, and the answer depends on age. In people under 60, the risk falls until about 8,000 to 10,000 steps a day. In those aged 60 and over, until about 6,000 to 8,000 steps.15 The authors judge that the benefit of walking faster, beyond the number of steps, remains inconsistent from one study to another.15

Another result points the same way, for leisure-time exercise. An analysis of more than half a million adults in the United States and Europe compares mortality with no leisure-time activity. Reaching 1 to 2 times the recommended minimum is associated with a 31% lower risk of death, and 3 to 5 times with a 39% reduction, the peak observed. At 10 times the minimum or more, neither additional benefit nor increased risk is observed.16 Participants reported their own activity.

For you: most of the benefit is gained quickly and the top of the curve is flat. You do not need to train like an athlete for health, and very high volumes do not appear dangerous. The step count includes all the walking you do in your day, that is, the movement that the chair replaces.

We now have a complete thread: a massive exposure, a measured association, an effect that diminishes with activity, a mechanism, a dose. What remains is to test its solidity by looking for what could distort it.

Step 6 of 6

What can distort all of this, and what remains uncertain

What we want to establish: the part of the result that withstands the objections, and the part that is not demonstrated.

Objection 1: reverse causation. A person who is coming down with an illness moves less, sits more, then dies earlier. The illness would then explain both the chair and the death. In the step meta-analysis, the researchers compared the studies according to their follow-up duration.15

The shorter the follow-up, the stronger the link appears, which suggests that illness plays a role

Adjusted hazard ratios, highest step quartile against lowest (intervals: 0.25 to 0.41 and 0.49 to 0.66). Source: Paluch et al., Lancet Public Health, 2022.15

What this means

When follow-up is short, the gap between the most active and the least active is much larger (0.32) than when it is long (0.57). This is what we would expect if some of the least active were already ill at the start. The association does not disappear for all that: at 6 years and more, it remains strong, with nearly 43% less risk (editorial calculation: 1 minus 0.57).15 The 2019 sensor study excluded deaths from the first two years, which changed the results little, but its authors judge that the bias may remain.8 Put plainly: part of the link is probably illness showing, not the chair acting, and another part holds up.

Objection 2: what is measured. Many figures come from questionnaires. The Biswas review notes that sedentary time is self-reported in all the articles but one.9 In Esteban, the authors acknowledge that self-report may overestimate moderate activity.7 Sensors have their limits too: the 2019 study analysed only the vertical axis, which may underestimate light activity, and step counters may differ by 20% or more.8,15

Objection 3: who it applies to. The sensor study covers adults aged 40 and over, in the United States and Western Europe, with a single measurement per person.8 The step meta-analysis includes only high-income countries, with mostly white volunteers.15 Nothing specific is established for 20-35 year-olds or for other regions of the world.

Objection 4: can the chair be corrected at the office? A Cochrane review (34 studies, 3,397 participants) finds that sit-stand desks reduce sitting time by 84 to 116 minutes during the working day, with very low-quality evidence. The effects on health remain unproven, and standing uses barely more energy than sitting.17

What does not exist. None of the work read here is a randomised trial that measured mortality in people who were asked to sit less or walk more. Causation at the level of death is not demonstrated. It is supported by the consistency of the results and by observed mechanisms.

The answer to the question

Answer

Your exercise sessions probably do not suffice, on their own, to neutralise a very long seated day. They matter a great deal, but according to the data read, your day also has to contain movement.

  • Solid. One adult in three moves too little (step 1). Sitting time is associated with a higher risk, with the same pattern in sensor studies, questionnaires and syntheses, and it rises faster beyond 8 to 9.5 hours a day (step 2). The risk falls as movement increases, and the biggest gain is at the start (step 5).
  • Probable. Activity reduces the effect of the chair: in the large Cambridge analysis, the excess risk linked to 8 hours or more sitting disappears at around 60 to 75 minutes of moderate activity a day, but this study is read in reports (step 3). A mechanism linked to sugar and insulin exists in short trials (step 4).
  • Not established. That the chair directly causes deaths. How much of the link comes from preceding illness. A precise figure for you, and what happens before age 40. That sit-stand desks or other workplace arrangements change health (step 6).

The answer to your question is therefore nuanced: exercise is necessary and very useful, but it does not suffice to compensate for an entirely seated day. The consequence is practical: you do not necessarily need to train more, you need to replace some sitting time with light movement, spread over the day, and break up long spells of sitting.

What to put in place

Dosed actions, in order. When a choice is practical and untested, it is said so.

  1. Measure your starting point during an ordinary week.Record your number of steps per day with a pedometer or a phone, always the same one, because devices may differ by 20% or more from one another. Also estimate your sitting time. The step studies rely on one week of measurement, enough to place your level.15 The test on this page assesses your fitness, not your sitting time: the two pieces of information complement each other.
  2. Add one step level before aiming high.The biggest gain lies between 3,500 and 5,800 steps, i.e. about 2,250 more steps a day.15 Aim for this level for a few weeks, then for 7,000 to 9,000 steps; the plateau observed is 8,000 to 10,000 steps before age 60.
  3. Break up long spells of sitting.The Dunstan trial tested 2 minutes of walking every 20 minutes.13 This rhythm has not been validated in real life; aim for at least a break of a few minutes every hour. This is a practical choice by the editorial team, not a threshold from a study.
  4. Replace sitting time with light movement.Calls while walking, stairs, getting off public transport a stop early. In the sensor study, the risk is lowest at around 375 minutes a day of light activity: an order of magnitude, not a mandatory target.8
  5. Keep your sessions.The WHO sets the guideline at 150 minutes of moderate activity a week, or 75 minutes of vigorous activity.1,2 Beyond that, the gain continues up to 3 to 5 times this guideline.16 If your day is very sedentary, 60 to 75 minutes a day is the level at which the excess risk disappears in the Cambridge analysis, walking included.11
  6. Take stock again every 8 to 12 weeks.Repeat the test on this page under the same conditions, and compare your average step count with your starting one. This frequency is a choice by the editorial team: none of the sources read sets one.

Chest pain, abnormal breathlessness or a known illness warrant medical advice before you move more intensely.

The limits of this article
  • Almost all the data are associations observed in adults aged 40 and over in rich countries. Several studies are read in an abstract or a report (list in the sources).
  • None of these figures measures your fitness: they describe what people do, not what their bodies can do.

Frequently asked questions

I exercise three times a week: am I protected from the chair?

In part. Three sessions count and put you at the public health guideline, but in the Cambridge analysis, the excess risk linked to 8 hours or more sitting disappeared only with 60 to 75 minutes of moderate activity a day.11 Active breaks during the day are therefore added to your sessions.

Does sitting time kill, or do sick people sit more?

Probably both. Part of the link comes from illness (gap between short and long follow-ups), another part holds up, and a mechanism exists in short trials.13,14,15 Proof of a direct cause is missing.

Is more always better?

Not for lifespan: the benefit appears to plateau around 3 to 5 times the recommended minimum, with no increased risk at 10 times and more.16 Nothing obliges you to train more for health alone.
